speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (a) what is the average duration between the time a mosquito breeding site is found and a fine is issued; (b) whether there have been instances where fines were found to have been issued to the wrong households upon appeal; and (c) if so, how many of such cases were there in the past three years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: More time is needed for cases that require further investigation and verification of the individual to be held accountable and issued with a fine.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Surges in the number of cases over the past few years, especially years with large dengue outbreaks, have led to longer processing times.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: My Ministry is currently reviewing the enforcement process with a view to reducing the time taken to issue a fine.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: These cases were rectified immediately when they were made known to NEA through feedback or appeals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: NEA will continue to monitor and improve its processes to avoid such errors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The reason why I am asking this Parliamentary Question (PQ) and these consequent supplementary questions is because I have been getting a number of residents complaining about letters coming in close to six months later, or a bit lengthier in some sense.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One resident told me that it is their first offence as well and they would not get fined again, but then found out eventually, six months later, that they got a fine in the letter box.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My Toa Payoh residents found this a bit worrying – six months after the fact.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And also, the fines are substantial and can be quite significant for some of the low-income residents in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first supplementary question, Mr Speaker is: can the letters be sent earlier?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think the Senior Parliamentary Secretary has highlighted that the Ministry is trying to work to reduce the timeframe.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the Ministry can hasten that a bit, it will be very useful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It can help in some ways, especially when the offence is initiated earlier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary give some details on how first offenders are treated in such cases, especially the first offenders, because they are not familiar with this?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, can there be instances where the letters can be handed over physically?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that there were four cases where wrong addresses were given to those who were fined.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think these are instances where the owner of the breeding sites is on the ground floor of a Housing and Development Board (HDB) block, for example, where the locations of the breeding sites could not be ascertained clearly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think there were some instances of that and whether we can avoid that, by handing over the letters physically in such cases and to check the ownership of the breeding sites.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Senior Parliamentary Secretary can share a bit on that.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: NEA's key priority is to make sure that dengue transmission is stopped.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, resources are devoted to detect and destroy breeding habitats.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: In fact, residents should be "happier", if they receive the fines later, so they have more time to respond to that.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But nevertheless, during dengue outbreak periods, there will be a lot more inspections and potentially more breeding grounds detected and, therefore, more fines and more administrative work to be done.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But we are committed to improving the processes so that residents do not have to wait too long to receive the fine.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The current practice is that when a breeding habitat is detected, a notification slip is given to the household.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: If the owner is not at home, the slip will be left at the household.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The slip will inform them that enforcement may be taken if the sample is verified to contain a vector.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: This slip will be issued when there are larvae found within the premises.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: NEA will remind its officers not to give this wrong impression that first timers will be let off more easily because dengue can cause fatality and we need everyone to play their part to keep mosquitoes at bay and to remove any potential breeding grounds.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Mr Saktiandi's second question is on the wrong address.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, if the owner is at home, the slip will be given.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But sometimes, there could be challenges or arguments as in, let us say, a pot along the common corridor.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It may not necessarily belong to the unit closest to it.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: That is where the resident who receives the notice can appeal and NEA will investigate and ascertain who is the rightful owner and the rightful party to be responsible for upkeeping the area.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: NEA will review all appeals properly on a case-by-case basis, depending on the situation and to exercise leniency where it is necessary.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The reason why I asked is because, for first offenders, they get it six months later, thinking that they were not supposed to be fined.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, I think the long duration exacerbated the concerns of the resident.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, my clarification is with regard to the notification slip.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share if the notification slip will be placed into the letter box or under the HDB flat unit's door?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, in what ways will the notifications be delivered?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: There could be cases where a household member returns home, may not understand what the slip is about and ignores it or throws it away.
